name: Startup Funding

claims.claim_text: Cree's co-founder recalls that the company's original capital came entirely from friends and family, raised in $5,000 personal checks written informally rather than through any institutional investor.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was basically talking to friends and family, going to a bar and sit there and someone writes you a check for $5,000.
claims.speaker: John Edmond
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Upverter's founders found that pooled personal savings bought them about four months before outside money was required, which is a realistic order of magnitude for a self-funded software-tool startup with three full-time founders.
claims.quote_verbatim: And that all lasted us about four months. And that was the first four months of the company.
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: A hardware company that raised roughly $250,000 from family and friends then attempted a $2 million seed round; escalating from a friends-and-family round to an institutional seed is the common next step, and it frequently fails.
claims.quote_verbatim: they raised a quarter of a million bucks from family and friends
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: For a hardware startup that is not doing something unusually capital-intensive, the up-front cost is measured in thousands rather than hundreds of thousands, which puts self-funding within reach of an ordinary engineering salary.
claims.quote_verbatim: And hardware, you know, unless you're doing something massively expensive, you know, you're only talking thousands
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: A concrete route to self-funding is to work three or four years after college, bank roughly fifty thousand dollars, and use that as a year of runway rather than raising outside money at the idea stage.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's possible to work for, you know, three or four years, you know, if you're out of college or something, work for three or four years and then save up the money.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: A revenue-funded growth loop for a small hardware product works by buying parts for a batch of roughly a hundred kits, selling them, and reinvesting the proceeds into a larger parts buy; it compounds slowly but never dilutes the founder.
claims.quote_verbatim: Buy a hundred kits worth of parts. Sell your hundred kits.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: A tinkering hobby was grown into a $33 million business with no outside funding at all, which stands as an existence proof that revenue-funded growth still reaches meaningful scale in hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: how one woman turned her passion for tinkering into a $33 million business without a dime of funding
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: The case for bootstrapping is control: while you are the only funder you own the whole company and answer to nobody, and that position is lost the moment external money arrives.
claims.quote_verbatim: you are the only funder at that point and you basically you own it all
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Kismetic Keithley Katowse

claims.claim_text: Raising money from a large crowd of small backers carries a hidden ongoing cost: a thousand people who each put in a thousand dollars become a thousand people expecting answers by email.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you take a thousand bucks from a thousand people
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kismetic Keithley Katowse

claims.claim_text: Having working prototypes in hand before seeking money puts a hardware startup ahead of the many that pitch on an idea alone, and self-funding those early prototypes is itself read as a positive signal.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fact that you guys are bootstrapping the early protos, that's a really good sign
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: A founder who wants to keep doing engineering cannot also run the fundraising process; taking charge of the company means the job becomes hunting for money, and that trade is not optional.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you want to keep being an engineer, you don't get to go hunting for money.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Standing With Ahmed

claims.claim_text: Fundraising is not a side activity that fits around a day job; founders who successfully raise typically report roughly twelve months of full-time effort spent finding someone willing to fund them.
claims.quote_verbatim: everyone we've spoken to, it's like, oh yeah, we've, you know, worked our ass off for, you know, 12 months trying to get somebody to fund us
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Standing With Ahmed

claims.claim_text: Expecting to raise money while continuing other full-time commitments is a common misjudgement; a serious raise requires clearing six months or more to devote to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't just do it on the side and think that, you know, somebody is just going to hand you money.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Standing With Ahmed

claims.claim_text: At the point of starting a company a founder faces a fork: fund it from personal savings or a personal bank loan and retain full ownership while carrying all the downside, or use investor money and shed personal risk at the cost of the company itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got a choice between, you know, leveraging your own funds, right? Or, you know, taking on that personal risk, getting your own loan from the bank, but you still own everything, or risking someone else's money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: A founder who has built and sold his own hardware business warns that bank debt is not a substitute for equity at the risky stage, because banks lend only against a guarantee of repayment rather than against the prospects of the venture.
claims.quote_verbatim: from the entrepreneur's side, you have to understand banks only loan money if they're guaranteed to be paid back.
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: Regional development foundations and civic funds are a real and underused source of startup capital; they are competitive and slow to win but generally attach far fewer strings than equity investors.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, if you're thinking about a startup, look for that kind of localized funding, because it's possible.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ludibrious Luxating Layout

claims.claim_text: The obligation attached to local foundation and civic startup money is usually publicity rather than equity or repayment: the funder wants to showcase the companies it backed as evidence its programme works.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only thing that's tied to it is, well, let us show off how awesome you are
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ludibrious Luxating Layout

claims.claim_text: Some national governments compete for startups by paying founders' living expenses to relocate for a fixed period, an arrangement that funds runway without taking any equity but requires physically moving the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: the government are trying to entice people to come to their actual startup companies to come to the country, and they'll help them out. So move to our country for six months, and we'll pay all your expenses.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ludibrious Luxating Layout

claims.claim_text: Before the JOBS Act, United States rules dating from the 1930s restricted private investment to family members and accredited angels who had to hold a million dollars in net worth excluding their home, which is why early rounds were confined to a small social circle.
claims.quote_verbatim: In order to be an angel investor, you have to have $1 million net worth, not including your house.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: The JOBS Act opened a path for a small startup to raise up to a million dollars in ten-thousand-dollar increments from investors who are not wealthy, with the company setting the equity terms for each increment.
claims.quote_verbatim: any small startup can get up to a million dollars in funding in $10,000 increments from small investors
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: A ban on general solicitation dating from 1933 meant that for most of the history of startups, fundraising had to happen privately; the practical consequence is that a founder's access to investors is limited to whoever is already in their network.
claims.quote_verbatim: finding a good investor is hard because you're limited by just the people that are immediately around you.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Finding investors at all is easy; the hard part is finding one who agrees with the direction you want to take the product, because a mismatched investor will pull the company somewhere else.
claims.quote_verbatim: startups have a hard time finding good investors. You can always find investors, but finding a good investor that is actually going to agree with what you think, take the product in the same direction as what you want.
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Y Combinator's standard offer at the time was $20,000 for about 7% of the company, with two three-month batches a year, in-person interviews and a same-evening decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're offered a spot, it's essentially $20,000 for what boils down to basically 7% of your company and your team.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: The accelerator application questions are worth answering even if you never apply, because they force a founder to state how the business will make money, how equity is split, and what they understand about the market that competitors do not.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like, how will you make money? What is the equity division? What are you understanding about this market that your competitors don't?
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: At the earliest stage, before manufacturing and unit cost matter, a hardware startup should not be materially slower than a software one; if any step such as populated boards or a printed enclosure is adding more than about a week, that is a process problem rather than an inherent property of hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: It shouldn't take you more than a week longer to do any aspect of your project at the earliest stages.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: A hardware accelerator based in Shenzhen offered $25,000 in seed funding that was expected to cover the founders' travel and living expenses on site as well as the company's costs, so the headline seed number was not all available for the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: I believe that the idea is that with the 25 K you cover your, your travel and living expenses as well over here.
claims.speaker: Zach Hoeken Smith
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Hoeken Smith - Creative China Commorant

claims.claim_text: An accelerator batch ends in a demo day where founders give a very short pitch to a room of investors; the actual raise happens in the weeks afterwards, so demo day is the start of the fundraising process rather than its conclusion.
claims.quote_verbatim: from that, you then, uh, you then attempt to raise investment in the kind of weeks
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Before getting into an accelerator, the founder of Snap EDA funded the company by freelancing as a writer for Reuters and Forbes and doing contract coding, which paid the bills but kept the product to part-time hours.
claims.quote_verbatim: because we didn't have any funding, I was working on other projects, right? I, well, I had to, I had to have an income. So I was writing for Reuters. I was writing for Forbes.
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: The founder of Snap EDA judged that the accelerator's most valuable effect was not the money itself but that a small amount of funding let her stop consulting and work on the company full time.
claims.quote_verbatim: what Y Combinator did is, you know, I always knew I wanted to do Snap EDA full time
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: A hardware founder who went through a general accelerator cautions that these programmes will not teach you hardware engineering; expect help with scaling and company-building, and treat technical instruction as out of scope.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't go to Y Combinator for them to teach you about hardware
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Reflecting on running CastAR, its founder concluded that a $1.5 million seed supporting a team of about ten was producing steady progress, and that the company would have been better served by a deliberate plan for how much to raise rather than taking the largest available round.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's also important to have, like, a really solid plan of how much money to raise. Like, I think we almost raised too much money because, you know, we raised $1.5 million in a seed round.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: After raising $15 million, CastAR grew from about ten to roughly twenty people in six months, far slower than the raise implied, which set up a mismatch between the capital taken and the pace the company could actually sustain.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then we raised $15 million. We only grew the team in the first six months to, like, 20-ish people.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: A large round comes with an expectation that the company will accelerate and start burning the money quickly; the size of the raise therefore dictates a growth rate, whether or not the product is ready for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the expectation was, after six months or so, it's like, you need to really be accelerating this company. And that's where you need to start burning this money fast.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: The venture-funded startup cycle assumes roughly annual raises, with each round sized to be exhausted in about a year; a company that spends its money more slowly than planned is counted as behind schedule rather than prudent.
claims.quote_verbatim: So like your cycle in a startup is raising money every single year ish.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: An investor who specialises in early hardware companies holds the counterintuitive position that raising too much money damages a startup more than raising too little.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually think it's, uh, worse to raise too much money than not enough money.
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A million dollars sounds large for a hardware startup but is consumed quickly once it covers founder and staff wages plus injection-mould tooling, which can run around fifty thousand dollars per mould.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you pay for molds at 50,000 bucks a pop or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: A million dollars of funding translates to roughly five people for one year if the company is not also manufacturing, which is the practical unit of account when sizing a raise against a development plan.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's five people if you're not building stuff or if you're not manufacturing. That's five people for a year.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: Even after a $15 million raise, a hardware company needed further capital specifically to fund the bill of materials for production, since inventory has to be paid for before any of it is sold.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we need money just for the bill of materials is one thing.
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: Alongside inventory, engineering salaries are the other dominant line item in a funded hardware company's spend, so a raise is largely a bet on how many engineer-years the product still needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: a big cost obviously is the engineering talent and salaries in general
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: Prototype PCB spending scales badly once boards get complex: quick-turn eight and ten layer prototypes ran about two thousand dollars for a single board.
claims.quote_verbatim: Like $2,000 for one board.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Grumpy Collaboration

claims.claim_text: Building a novel electric propulsion system on startup money, the team kept capital costs down by improvising: the first hollow cathode was housed in an off-the-shelf plumbing pipe rather than custom hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: our first cathode looked like a home depot plumbing pipe because it was a home depot plumbing pipe
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: A startup built its own vacuum chamber reaching ten to the minus five torr for about fifteen thousand dollars, far below the commercial cost, because a founder with prior experience fabricated it in house.
claims.quote_verbatim: we built a vacuum chamber that would get down to Mark really built a vacuum chamber that would get down to 10 to the minus five tour for like $15,000
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: Electric Propulsion with Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Running a small hardware company on limited capital, the founder of Cartesian Co made a discipline of asking what the cheapest apparatus is that can test the current hypothesis, rather than buying laboratory equipment to do it properly.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than, than build a whole big apparatus and buy a whole bunch of expensive scientific measuring equipment, what's the simplest possible way we can do it
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: The founders of CastAR delayed moving to larger office space longer than was comfortable because they were afraid of running out of money, which is a common and rational instinct in an early funded company.
claims.quote_verbatim: Rick and I were both, like, petrified of running out of money
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Facing a reality check, Upverter's founders compared their bank balance against the work remaining and found they had about one third of the money required, before even accounting for the likelihood of running late.
claims.quote_verbatim: we looked at the bank balance and we had about a third as much money as we needed to get to what we thought it was going to take
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: The decision point in a funded startup arrives when the cash covers four or five months and the remaining work will take eight; at that moment the options are to pivot, to go back to investors, or to wind up and return the money.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can get, you know, four or five months out of this money and it's probably going to take us eight
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Upverter finished its accelerator with $450,000 of external money, planned as twelve months of runway for a modest hiring plan; the round was sized directly against what the team intended to accomplish.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I roll everything up at the end of Y Combinator, we had $450,000 in external money. And that was enough. Like, at the time, that was enough for 12 months.
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: By stretching spending well past the original plan, Upverter ran three years of company operation on about $650,000 of total raised capital before taking its first institutional round.
claims.quote_verbatim: in June, we had only raised $650,000, give or take. And that had lasted us three years.
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Companies rarely wind down gradually; the money runs out abruptly, and a company can go from operating normally to having a week of cash and no incoming investment.
claims.quote_verbatim: like the money literally runs out overnight or, you know, like we've, we've got a week's worth of money left and there's no more investment.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Automation Amish

claims.claim_text: A distressed company usually cannot admit publicly that it is near bankruptcy, because signalling that position destroys any price it might get in a sale; outsiders should therefore not read silence as health.
claims.quote_verbatim: nobody wants to admit to anyone that they're on the brink of bankruptcy
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The EEVblog Sparkgap Generator

claims.claim_text: An engineer who has worked at several startups advises keeping three to five months of personal living expenses in savings before joining one, because layoffs and pay cuts arrive with no warning when a round fails to close.
claims.quote_verbatim: this advice for anybody is like have at least three to five months of expenses and savings
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Asking a startup about its cash position is not enough, because a company with two years of runway will not spend down to zero: expect a round of cuts at the one-year mark and another at six months as management stretches the money.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you have a company that has like a two year runway, they don't want to use it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Before joining a startup, ask about its cash flow situation and its runway rather than its headline funding total, since cash on hand says nothing about the rate at which it will be spent.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was advised many times to ask about their cash flow situation, ask about like what's their runway
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: An engineer who left a stable instrument-company job for a hardware startup found it out of money four months after he joined, and then continued working there accruing shares instead of a salary.
claims.quote_verbatim: I stayed on afterwards, you know, accruing shares, um, instead of money.
claims.speaker: Dave Young
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Having tried to fund silicon development from a crowdfunding campaign, Adapteva's founder concluded that when reaching a shipping product plus a software ecosystem costs millions, bootstrapping is not a realistic option.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you need millions of dollars to reach a product and an ecosystem, it's hard to do that.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: A working prototype is the instrument that unlocks funding, and funding in turn is what makes it possible to hire the specialists and support staff needed to make the product good.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have a prototype, which allows you to shop it around and then you get funding and then you can afford the super experts as well
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: A hardware founder distinguishes two viable kinds of hardware startup that need different funding: brand-led consumer products that can grow explosively and be sold quickly, and long-horizon deep-technology companies whose payoff is far away.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's, there's two types of hardware, hardware startups that are, uh, viable and they take different funding.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Silicon Valley chip companies were once routinely funded to Series C or D before any revenue at all, a pattern that no longer exists and which explains why deep-technology hardware is now much harder to finance.
claims.quote_verbatim: many of those companies that I was working at were at like Series C or D fundraising before they actually saw revenue, which is almost unheard of.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: A semiconductor founder reports that even an experienced team with a good reputation found it extremely hard to raise the capital to build a chip company, which is the practical barrier behind the decline of venture-backed semiconductor startups.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you go back to the story I told at the beginning of how hard it was for us to get our funding, and we were a pretty experienced group with a pretty good reputation.
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Having raised venture money to build a semiconductor company to scale, the founder judged his to be among the last that would be funded that way.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think we are the last or one of the last semiconductor companies that you're really going to see that's venture-backed, that's going to build to scale.
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Investors looking at consumer electronics and open hardware companies reportedly would not engage below a ten million dollar threshold, leaving a gap where a company is too large for small-company tactics and too small to attract that capital.
claims.quote_verbatim: They won't even talk to you if you're less than 10 million, they said.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Altera was started in 1983 on $750,000 of secured funding, a useful benchmark for what it once cost to launch a programmable-logic semiconductor company.
claims.quote_verbatim: These four people secured $750,000 in funding in 1983 to start Altera.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Altium...Acquired!

claims.claim_text: Recalling his own dot-com-era company, Eric Ries describes an environment where any plausible-sounding idea attracted a couple of million dollars, and where that easy money funded a product nobody ultimately wanted.
claims.quote_verbatim: In the dot-com era, it seemed like if you had indigestion and it felt like a good idea, people said, yeah, here's a couple million.
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: An inventor mortgaged her house and put roughly a quarter of a million dollars of her own money into a product that was already being sold by many others, illustrating why a competitive search should precede any self-funded commitment of that size.
claims.quote_verbatim: I mortgaged my house and put like a quarter of a million dollars into this idea
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The EEVblog Sparkgap Generator

attribution_notes: Passage 3 (ep 71) is labelled Chris Gammell in the diarised transcript, but the content is the guest, Cree co-founder John Edmond, answering Dave Jones's direct question about how the company got its capital funding; attributed to John Edmond by content.

Passages 10-11 (ep 87) are labelled Ian Danaher, but the speaker explains the JOBS Act and says he 'could invest $10,000 into Ian's startup', so the speaker cannot be Ian Danaher; attributed to Chris Gammell, who introduced the topic.

Passages 26-28 (ep 163) carry the diarisation label SPEAKER_03. The content identifies the speaker as the Upverter co-founder who had student debt while Steve Hamer and Michael Woodworth contributed personal savings, i.e. Zach Homet; attributed accordingly.
Passage 55 (ep 268) is labelled 'Y Combinator' by the diariser; the content is Luke Iseman describing the programme from the inside and is attributed to him.

Passage 57 (ep 305) is labelled Chris Gammell in the transcript, but the narration is answered with 'How much are the shares worth, Dave?' and is the guest's own career story; attributed to Dave Young. Both men worked at Keithley, which is why the diarisation is ambiguous here.
Passage 46 (ep 260): the 'simplest possible way' material is labelled Chris Gammell but describes Cartesian Co's own development method and is attributed to its founder Ariel Briner by content.

Passage 48 (ep 260): the extended explanation of 1933 general-solicitation law is labelled Chris Gammell, but the guest Ariel Briner had raised the legality of discussing startup fundraising and the diarisation in this stretch is demonstrably unreliable (it also invents a separate 'Ariel Of Cartesian Co' speaker). The content does not settle which of the two is speaking, so speaker is left as None.
Passages 61-62 (ep 368) are flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE; speakers were re-derived from the transcript labels immediately preceding each quoted span.
Passages 64-68 (ep 394) are labelled 'Jerry Ellsworth' in the transcript; normalised to Jeri Ellsworth.
Passage 19 (ep 121) is labelled 'Zach Hoken'; normalised to Zach Hoeken Smith.

Passage 60 (ep 351) and passage 80 (ep 563): quoted spans were confirmed against the transcript speaker labels, which give Dave Jones in both cases despite adjacent material belonging to Chris Gammell.
Passage 76 (ep 509): the three-to-five-months-savings advice is Jared Wolff's; the runway-and-chops material immediately following it is Chris Gammell's, confirmed from the transcript labels.
